answer_to_user:
All three converted to USD (as-of FY2026-06-30):
• Toyota (7203.JP): revenue ~$336.9B, net income ~$25.6B, operating margin 7.0%, ROE 12.0%, net debt ~$192B (total debt $272B − cash $80B); net_debt/EBITDA 3.87x, debt/equity 1.18x.
• Volkswagen (VOW.XETRA): revenue ~$364.1B, net income ~$8.3B, operating margin 4.4%, ROE 4.5%, net debt ~$185B (debt $231B − cash $46B); net_debt/EBITDA 3.03x, debt/equity 1.06x. FCF was negative (−$10.6B).
• General Motors (GM.US): revenue ~$185.0B, net income ~$2.7B, operating margin 1.0%, ROE 3.1%, net debt ~$110B (debt $131B − cash $21B); net_debt/EBITDA 6.14x, debt/equity 2.06x.

Strongest balance sheet: TOYOTA. It has the highest profitability (op margin 7%, ROE 12%) and, critically, the lowest leverage — debt/equity 1.18x and it generated positive FCF, versus VW (negative FCF, op margin 4.4%) and GM (debt/equity 2.06x, net_debt/EBITDA 6.1x, ROE just 3.1%). VW screens cheaper on multiples but is burning cash; GM is the most levered and least profitable. All figures normalized to USD so magnitudes are comparable; ratios (margin, ROE) are currency-neutral. (Note: absolute net-debt magnitudes for auto OEMs include large captive-finance debt, so the RATIOS are the cleaner balance-sheet read — and there Toyota wins.)
